body:
Industrial robots

Industrial robots carry out tasks in manufacturing and related industrial environments. Many are programmable manipulators consisting of connected mechanical segments and joints. They can be used for repetitive handling, welding, painting, assembly, packaging and inspection when equipped for the required task.

An industrial robot is useful where consistent repetition, suitable positioning and operation in difficult conditions are important. However, a robot does not automatically improve every process. The task must be suitable, and equipment, maintenance, human supervision and safety arrangements remain necessary.

Service and medical robotics

Service robots perform useful tasks for people or equipment outside the usual industrial-manipulator setting. Examples include robotic vacuum cleaners, delivery robots, cleaning machines for public buildings and inspection robots. Some operate with substantial independence, while others require supervision.

Medical robotic systems can assist with surgery, rehabilitation, diagnosis or other healthcare tasks. A robot-assisted surgical system may translate the surgeon's commands into controlled movements. This does not mean that the robot independently diagnoses the patient or decides to perform an operation. Under ISO 8373:2021, medical robots are recognised separately from industrial and service robots.

Agricultural robotics and drones

Agriculture can use robotic and automated machines for crop observation, targeted application of inputs, harvesting or field monitoring. An uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV), commonly called a drone, can carry cameras or other equipment. Depending on the system, it may be manually piloted, assisted by automated functions or capable of following a predefined flight path.

A drone is not automatically a fully autonomous aircraft. Its practical operation depends on the task, equipment, trained operator and applicable aviation and agricultural requirements. A drone that takes photographs is collecting information; a drone fitted with an authorised spraying system can also perform a physical agricultural task.

Indian examples in space and defence

India's Chandrayaan-3 mission included the Pragyan rover, demonstrating a mobile robotic application in space exploration. ISRO identifies 2 scientific instruments on the rover: the Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) and the Laser Induced Breakdown Spectroscope (LIBS). Both were intended to investigate the elemental composition of material near the lunar landing site.

Space robots are valuable because the environment may be remote, hazardous or inaccessible to people. Robotic systems can also be used for scientific inspection, disaster response and other difficult tasks. Such machines may combine programmed activity with commands sent by human operators.

In defence and public safety, remotely operated devices can assist personnel in inspecting potentially hazardous objects or locations while reducing the need for close human exposure. India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has developed the DAKSH remotely operated robotic system for hazardous-object handling. Remote operation must not be mistaken for complete autonomy.

Benefits and limitations

Robotic systems can improve repeatability, assist with physically demanding work and permit operations in hazardous or inaccessible areas. Their limitations include cost, dependence on power and maintenance, restrictions of sensors and programs, and the need for human accountability. Deployment should be judged by the actual task rather than by the assumption that every robot is more capable than a human worker.

Prelims focus

  • Industrial robots commonly perform manufacturing tasks such as handling, welding and assembly.
  • Service robots perform useful tasks for people or equipment.
  • ISO 8373:2021 distinguishes medical robots as a separate category.
  • Chandrayaan-3 included the Pragyan rover.
  • Pragyan carried APXS and LIBS for elemental analysis.
  • Trap: A remotely piloted drone or remotely operated robotic device is not necessarily autonomous.

[Sources: International Federation of Robotics, Industrial Robots and Service Robots, ISO 8373:2021 definitions and application categories, accessed 2026-11-05; NCERT, Informatics Practices, Class 11, Chapter 2, section 2.2.4, accessed 2026-11-05; ISRO, Chandrayaan-3 Details, rover payloads and mission objectives, accessed 2026-11-05; Press Information Bureau, Pride of India Expo Attracts Huge Crowd, 4 January 2010, section on DRDO exhibits, accessed 2026-11-05.]

body:
Why safety is essential in robotics

A robot may move heavy components, operate machinery or travel near people. Its movements can create risks if a person enters its operating area, an obstacle is not detected, a command is incorrect or the equipment develops a fault. Robotic safety means reducing such risks through suitable equipment, procedures and human oversight.

A machine working correctly according to its program is not necessarily safe in every situation. The environment may change, a sensor may give an incorrect reading or a person may behave unexpectedly. Safety therefore requires more than accurate programming.

Common safety measures

  • Physical separation and guarding: Keep people away from hazardous robot movements where appropriate.
  • Obstacle and presence detection: Use suitable sensors to detect people or objects within relevant areas.
  • Emergency stopping: Provide a means to bring hazardous movement to a stop when necessary. An emergency stop is a protective measure, not a replacement for safe system design.
  • Speed and movement limits: Restrict movement according to the task and its operating environment.
  • Training and supervision: Ensure that people understand the machine's operating limits and the required precautions.
  • Maintenance and fault handling: Check for failures that may affect sensing, power, movement or control.

Collaborative robots

A collaborative robot, often called a cobot, is intended for suitable forms of human-robot interaction in a shared working environment. Such applications may use features including limited force, monitored movement or protective stopping.

However, the word collaborative does not mean that every robot, tool or operation is automatically safe to touch. The safety of a collaborative application depends on the complete arrangement, including the attached tool, task, operating conditions and protective measures.

Failure of sensors, power or communication

Robotic systems should respond appropriately when information or control becomes unreliable. A mobile robot might need to stop if it cannot reliably determine whether its path is clear. A remotely operated device may need a defined safe response if communication with its operator is interrupted.

A system may also need to distinguish between an ordinary operating stop and an emergency condition. In both cases, the objective is to prevent hazardous movement or another unsafe outcome. The exact response depends on the machine and its application.

Cybersecurity and physical safety

Connecting a robot to a network creates additional possibilities for monitoring and coordination, but it can also create cybersecurity risks. An unauthorised command, altered settings or interrupted communication may affect a connected robot's physical behaviour. Appropriate access controls and secure maintenance therefore support both information security and physical safety.

In healthcare, disaster response and other high-consequence applications, automation should not be confused with the removal of professional responsibility. A trained human may still need to supervise decisions, handle exceptions and ensure appropriate action.

Prelims focus

  • Robot safety includes protective equipment, operating limits and human procedures.
  • Emergency stopping is one protective measure, not a complete safety system.
  • A collaborative robot is not automatically safe for every task.
  • Sensor failure can affect the correctness of a robot's response.
  • Network security matters when digital commands can affect physical movement.
  • Trap: Successful automation does not eliminate the need for human accountability or supervision.

[Sources: International Federation of Robotics, Industrial Robots and Service Robots, definitions and application context, accessed 2026-11-05; NIST, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline, NISTIR 8259A, May 2020, device configuration, access and data-protection capabilities, accessed 2026-11-05; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Control and Coordination, section 6.1, consulted in GPSC textbook compendium volume 32.]

pictures.caption: Different faults require appropriate protective responses and supervision.

title: Robotic Safety, Human Supervision and System Reliability

body:
What makes a system part of the Internet of Things?

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a system of connected physical or virtual things that use communication technologies to exchange information and support useful services. The things may include electricity meters, agricultural monitoring devices, machines, vehicles, household appliances and other identifiable objects.

According to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), communication is a required capability of an IoT device, while sensing, actuation, data storage and data processing are additional capabilities that may or may not be present. Therefore, an IoT device does not always need both a sensor and an actuator.

In ordinary applications, IoT makes information about physical conditions available to other devices, computer platforms or authorised users. Some systems also allow control commands to be sent back to devices.

The main parts of an IoT system

  • Connected thing or device: The equipment that is identified and communicates within the system.
  • Sensor or data source: Obtains useful information such as temperature, soil moisture, location or electricity consumption, when required.
  • Communication network: Carries information between devices, gateways and other systems.
  • Gateway: May connect a local device network to another network and translate between communication methods.
  • Platform or application: Receives, stores, displays and processes data for monitoring, analysis, alerts or control.
  • Actuator: Produces a physical action when the application requires one, such as operating a valve or motor.

Example: a connected irrigation system

Consider a farm where a soil-moisture sensor measures the moisture condition near crop roots. A connected device transmits the reading to a controller or monitoring platform. If the reading meets a programmed condition and irrigation is permitted, the controller may command a pump or valve to operate. Further measurements help determine whether watering should continue.

Such a system can help the farmer make more informed irrigation decisions. However, a moisture reading does not by itself determine every agricultural requirement. Crop type, soil conditions, weather and the suitability of the programmed settings also matter.

Monitoring and control are different outcomes

An IoT monitoring system may only collect and report information. For example, a connected air-quality monitor can transmit readings without changing the surrounding air. An IoT control system can additionally send commands to equipment, such as switching on ventilation under appropriate conditions.

Data transmission need not be continuous. Some connected devices transmit readings at intervals, while others report when a particular event occurs. Devices may also store data temporarily if communication is unavailable and transmit it later when the system supports that function.

An electronic device is not automatically an IoT device. A basic digital thermometer that only displays temperature locally is an electronic measuring instrument. A thermometer that can communicate its readings to other systems may serve as part of an IoT application.

Prelims focus

  • IoT combines identifiable things with communication and useful information exchange.
  • Sensing and actuation are common but not compulsory capabilities of every IoT device.
  • A gateway may connect different networks and translate communication protocols.
  • Monitoring reports a condition; control can also command an action.
  • IoT data may be transmitted periodically or when an event occurs.
  • Trap: Every digital sensor, by itself, is not an IoT system.

[Sources: ITU-T Recommendation Y.4218, Internet of Things and Information and Communication Technology Requirements for Deployment of Smart Services in Rural Communities, May 2023, sections 3.1.1–3.1.3, accessed 2026-11-05; NCERT, Informatics Practices, Class 11, Chapter 2, sections 2.4, 2.4.2 and 2.4.3, accessed 2026-11-05; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Crop Production and Management, section 1.6, consulted in GPSC textbook compendium volume 30.]

pictures.alt: Moisture readings reach a controller and farmer; permitted programmed conditions may trigger a pump or valve, with further readings providing feedback.

title: Internet of Things: Meaning, Components and Working Principle

body:
Why connectivity matters

An IoT device must communicate information so that another device or system can use it. The communication method depends on the required distance, available infrastructure, power supply, quantity of data and reliability needed for the application.

Communication can use a wired connection or a wireless connection. A short-range sensor in a building may use a local wireless network. A field device located far from a control room may require a different technology. No single method is best for every IoT application.

Common connection technologies

TechnologyTypical characteristicExample use
EthernetWired local networkingFixed industrial equipment
Wi-FiWireless local networking with relatively high data capacityConnected home appliances or cameras
Bluetooth Low EnergyShort-range communication designed for low-power applicationsWearable sensors
ZigbeeLow-power local networkingBuilding sensors and smart lighting
LoRaWANLong-range, low-data-rate communicationDistributed environmental sensors
Cellular networksCommunication through mobile-network infrastructure, including suitable IoT servicesConnected vehicles and remote meters

Technologies such as 4G, 5G and Narrowband IoT (NB-IoT) belong to the wider cellular communication family, although they are designed for different service requirements. NB-IoT is particularly associated with communication from devices that send relatively small amounts of data.

What does an IoT gateway do?

A gateway links devices to communication networks and may translate information between different protocols. For example, several building sensors may communicate locally with a gateway. The gateway can then forward their readings through another network to a monitoring platform.

A gateway is not compulsory in every arrangement. Some devices can connect directly through a suitable network, while others depend on a gateway because their local communication method differs from that used by the wider network.

Communication networks and application protocols

A network technology provides a means of carrying information. An application protocol specifies how an application exchanges messages. These are different concepts.

For example, HTTP commonly supports exchanges based on a request and a response. MQTT is a lightweight messaging protocol frequently used in IoT applications. Its publish-subscribe approach allows a sender to publish information under a topic and interested recipients to receive relevant messages through a messaging broker.

The learner need not memorise software implementation details to understand the distinction. Wi-Fi and cellular technology concern network connectivity; HTTP and MQTT concern the organisation of application messages.

Does IoT always require a continuous Internet connection?

An IoT system may use local networks, gateways and wider Internet-based services in different combinations. Some functions can operate locally, and some devices can buffer readings during an interruption. Nevertheless, communication remains central to the concept of IoT. A completely isolated device that never exchanges information with other systems should not be described as part of a functioning IoT arrangement merely because it contains electronics.

Prelims focus

  • Wi-Fi and Ethernet are networking technologies.
  • Bluetooth Low Energy is associated with short-range, low-power communication.
  • LoRaWAN is associated with long-range, low-data-rate applications.
  • NB-IoT belongs to cellular IoT communication technologies.
  • MQTT is an application messaging protocol, not a satellite-navigation system.
  • Trap: A gateway is useful for interconnecting different networks but is not compulsory for every IoT device.

[Sources: ITU-T Recommendation Y.4218, May 2023, section 3.1, device and gateway definitions, accessed 2026-11-05; ITU-T Recommendation Y.4101, Requirements for IoT Gateway, October 2017, overview, accessed 2026-11-05; ITU-T Recommendation Y.4235, September 2025, descriptions of IoT communication and MQTT, accessed 2026-11-05; NCERT, Informatics Practices, Class 11, Chapter 2, section 2.4, accessed 2026-11-05.]

pictures.caption: IoT devices can communicate directly or through a gateway.
